title: Chandogya Upanishad, Prapathaka 1 (the udgitha and the syllable Om)
source: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 945 (OPenn, public domain) + GRETIL Sanskrit + F. Max Müller (1879) English
description: Chapter 1 of the Chandogya Upanishad in Sanskrit and Max Müller's English, each passage linked to the page of a Sanskrit manuscript of the whole Upanishad at the University of Pennsylvania (Ms. Coll. 390 Item 945).
introduction:
The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Samaveda and is one of the two longest and oldest Upanishads. It has eight chapters (prapathakas). This entry gives chapter 1. It opens the Upanishad with meditations on the udgitha, the chanted portion of a Saman, identified with the syllable Om. It tells how the gods used the udgitha against the demons, how the priests Silaka, Caikitayana and the king Pravahana Jaivali debated the support of the Saman, how the impoverished Usasti Cakrayana challenged the priests at a royal sacrifice, and closes with the 'udgitha of the dogs' and the stobha syllables.

The page images come from University of Pennsylvania Libraries, Ms. Coll. 390 Item 945, a paper manuscript of 74 leaves (11 x 17 cm) holding the whole Chandogya Upanishad, written in Devanagari, 10 to 11 lines to a side, on blue machine-made paper with watermarks; it is undated (catalogued 18th or 19th century). The scribe numbers the khandas and closes each chapter with a colophon, but does not number paragraphs. Chapter 1 runs from fol. 1v to fol. 12r.

For every page, the first and last words were read on the image and found in the edited text; the page boundaries follow from them. Each section below holds the paragraphs that end on one page, with every page they occupy.
translator_notes: Sanskrit: GRETIL, Chandogyopanisad with the commentary ascribed to Samkara, mula text only (input by the Sansknet project). Paragraph numbers (khanda.paragraph) follow the edition. Three legacy encoding artifacts in GRETIL chapter 2 ('saptavidh.am', 'brahmavarcasy:', 'tejasvy:') are normalized.

English: F. Max Müller, 'Khandogya-upanishad', The Upanishads part I, Sacred Books of the East 1 (1879), from the proofread English Wikisource transcription; footnotes are not reproduced. Where Müller divides a khanda into a different number of paragraphs than the Sanskrit edition, the whole khanda stands in one section and keeps his numbers. In other khandas his paragraph breaks sometimes fall a clause earlier or later than the Sanskrit ones.

Transcription slips corrected to the printed page: 1.9.2 'udîttha' (printed udgîtha), 3.16.2 'sacrifices' (sacrificer,), 4.6.1 'toward' (towards), 7.25.1 'alt' (all); the stray heading 'Elventh Khanda' inside 2.10.6 is removed. 1.2.1 'Whent he' is a misprint in the book itself and is kept as printed.

translation.text:
1.1Let a man meditate on the syllable Om, called the udgîtha; for the udgîtha (a portion of the Sâma-veda) is sung, beginning with Om. The full account, however, of Om is this:—
1.2The essence of all beings is the earth, the essence of the earth is water, the essence of water the plants, the essence of plants man, the essence of man speech, the essence of speech the Rig-veda, the essence of the Rig-veda the Sâma-veda, the essence of the Sâma-veda the udgîtha (which is Om).
1.3That udgîtha (Om) is the best of all essences, the highest, deserving the highest place, the eighth.
1.4What then is the Rik? What is the Sâman? What is the udgîtha? This is the question.
1.5The Rik indeed is speech, Sâman is breath, the udgîtha is the syllable Om. Now speech and breath, or Rik and Sâman, form one couple.

translation.text:
1.6And that couple is joined together in the syllable Om. When two people come together, they fulfil each other's desire.
1.7Thus he who knowing this, meditates on the syllable (Om), the udgîtha, becomes indeed a fulfiller of desires.
1.8That syllable is a syllable of permission, for whenever we permit anything, we say Om, yes. Now permission is gratification. He who knowing this meditates on the syllable (Om), the udgîtha, becomes indeed a gratifier of desires.
1.9By that syllable does the threefold knowledge (the sacrifice, more particularly the Soma-sacrifice, as founded on the three Vedas) proceed. When the Adhvaryu priest gives an order, he says Om. When the Hotri priest recites, he says Om. When the Udgâtri priest sings, he says Om, —all for the glory of that syllable. The threefold knowledge (the sacrifice) proceeds by the greatness of that syllable (the vital breaths), and by its essence (the oblations).

translation.text:
1.10Now therefore it would seem to follow, that both he who knows this (the true meaning of the syllable Om), and he who does not, perform the same sacrifice. But this is not so, for knowledge and ignorance are different. The sacrifice which a man performs with knowledge, faith, and the Upanishad is more powerful. This is the full account of the syllable Om.
2.1Whent he Devas and Asuras struggled together, both of the race of Pragâpati, the Devas took the udgîtha (Om), thinking they would vanquish the Asuras with it.
2.2They meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as the breath (scent) in the nose, but the Asuras pierced it (the breath) with evil. Therefore we smell by the breath in the nose both what is good-smelling and what is bad-smelling. For the breath was pierced by evil.
2.3Then they meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as speech, but the Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore we speak both truth and falsehood. For speech is pierced by evil.
2.4Then they meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as the eye, but the Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore we see both what is sightly and unsightly. For the eye is pierced by evil.

translation.text:
2.5Then they meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as the ear, but the Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore we hear both what should be heard and what should not be heard. For the ear is pierced by evil.
2.6Then they meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as the mind, but the Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore we conceive both what should be conceived and what should not be conceived. For the mind is pierced by evil.
2.7Then comes this breath (of life) in the mouth. They meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as that breath. When the Asuras came to it, they were scattered, as (a ball of earth) would be scattered when hitting a solid stone.
2.8Thus, as a ball of earth is scattered when hitting on a solid stone, will he be scattered who wishes evil to one who knows this, or who persecutes him; for he is a solid stone.
2.9By it (the breath in the mouth) he distinguishes neither what is good nor what is bad-smelling, for that breath is free from evil. What we eat and drink with it supports the other vital breaths (i. e. the senses, such as smell, &c.) When at the time of death he does not find that breath (in the mouth, through which he eats and drinks and lives), then he departs. He opens the mouth at the time of death (as if wishing to eat).

translation.text:
2.10Angiras meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as that breath, and people hold it to be Angiras, i. e. the essence of the members (angânâm rasah);
2.11Therefore Brihaspati meditated on udgîtha (Om) as that breath, and people hold it to be Brihaspati, for speech is brihatî, and he (that breath) is the lord (pati) of speech;
2.12Therefore Ayâsya meditated on the udgîtha (Om) as that breath, and people hold it to be Ayâsya, because it comes (ayati) from the mouth (âsya);
2.13Therefore Vaka Dâlbhya knew it. He was the Udgâtri (singer) of the Naimishîya-sacrificers, and by singing he obtained for them their wishes.
2.14He who knows this, and meditates on the syllable Om (the imperishable udgîtha) as the breath of life in the mouth, he obtains all wishes by singing. So much for the udgîtha (Om) as meditated on with reference to the body.
3.1Now follows the meditation on the udgîtha with reference to the gods. Let a man meditate on the udgîtha (Om) as he who sends warmth (the sun in the sky). When the sun rises it sings as Udgâtri for the sake of all creatures. When it rises it destroys the fear of darkness. He who knows this, is able to destroy the fear of darkness (ignorance).
3.2This (the breath in the mouth) and that (the sun) are the same. This is hot and that is hot. This they call svara (sound), and that they call pratyâsvara (reflected sound). Therefore let a man meditate on the udgîtha (Om) as this and that (as breath and as sun).
3.3Then let a man meditate on the udgîtha (Om) as vyâna indeed. If we breathe up, that is prâna, the up-breathing. If we breathe down, that is apâna, the down-breathing. The combination of prâna and apâna is vyâna, back-breathing or holding in of the breath. This vyâna is speech. Therefore when we utter speech, we neither breathe up nor down.
3.4Speech is Rik, and therefore when a man utters a Rik verse he neither breathes up nor down. Rik is Sâman, and therefore when a man utters a Sâman verse he neither breathes up nor down. Sâman is udgîtha, and therefore when a man sings (the udgîtha, Om) he neither breathes up nor down.
3.5And other works also which require strength, such as the production of fire by rubbing, running a race, stringing a strong bow, are performed without breathing up or down. Therefore let a man meditate on the udgîtha (Om) as vyâna.
3.6Let a man meditate on the syllables of the udgîtha, i. e. of the word udgîtha. Ut is breath (prâna), for by means of breath a man rises (uttishthati). Gî is speech, for speeches are called girah. Tha is food, for by means of food all subsists (sthita).
3.7Ut is heaven, gî the sky, tha the earth. Ut is the sun, gî the air, tha the fire. Ut is the Sâma-veda, gî the Yagur-veda, tha the Rig-veda. Speech yields the milk, which is the milk of speech itself, to him who thus knowing meditates on those syllables of the name of udgîtha, he becomes rich in food and able to eat food.
3.8Next follows the fulfilment of prayers. Let a man thus meditate on the Upasaranas, i. e. the objects which have to be approached by meditation: Let him (the Udgâtri) quickly reflect on the Sâman with which he is going to praise;
3.9Let him quickly reflect on the Rik in which that Sâman occurs; on the Rishi (poet) by whom it was seen or composed; on the Devatâ (object) which he is going to praise;
3.10On the metre in which he is going to praise; on the tune with which he is going to sing for himself;
3.11On the quarter of the world which he is going to praise. Lastly, having approached himself (his name, family, &c.) by meditation, let him sing the hymn of praise, reflecting on his desire, and avoiding all mistakes in pronunciation, &c. Quickly will the desire be then fulfilled to him, for the sake of which he may have offered his hymn of praise, yea, for which he may have offered his hymn of praise.
4.1Let a man meditate on the syllable Om, for the udgîtha is sung beginning with Om. And this is the full account of the syllable Om:—
4.2The Devas, being afraid of death, entered upon (the performance of the sacrifice prescribed in) the threefold knowledge (the three Vedas). They covered themselves with the metrical hymns. Because they covered (khad) themselves with the hymns, therefore the hymns are called khandas.
4.3Then, as a fisherman might observe a fish in the water, Death observed the Devas in the Rik, Yagus, and Sâman-(sacrifices). And the Devas seeing this, rose from the Rik, Yagus, and Sâman-sacrifices, and entered the Svara, i.e. the Om (they meditated on the Om).

4.4When a man has mastered the Rig-veda, he says quite loud Om; the same, when he has mastered the Sâman and the Yagus. This Svara is the imperishable (syllable), the immortal, free from fear. Because the Devas entered it, therefore they became immortal, and free from fear.
4.5He who knowing this loudly pronounces (pranauti) that syllable, enters the same (imperishable) syllable, the Svara, the immortal, free from fear, and having entered it, becomes immortal, as the Devas are immortal.
5.1The udgîtha is the pranava, the pranava is the udgîtha. And as the udgîtha is the sun, so is the pranava, for he (the sun) goes sounding Om.
5.2'Him I sang praises to, therefore art thou my only one,' thus said Kaushîtaki to his son. 'Do thou revolve his rays, then thou wilt have many sons.' So much in reference to the Devas.
5.3Now with reference to the body. Let a man meditate on the udgîtha as the breath (in the mouth), for he goes sounding Om.
5.4'Him I sang praises to, therefore art thou my only son,' thus said Kaushîtaki to his son. 'Do thou therefore sing praises to the breath as manifold, if thou wishest to have many sons.'

8.5'What is the origin of water?' 'That world (heaven),' he replied. 'And what is the origin of that world?'— He replied: 'Let no man carry the Sâman beyond the world of svarga (heaven). We place (recognise) the Sâman in the world of svarga, for the Sâman is extolled as svarga (heaven).'
8.6Then said Silaka Sâlâvatya to Kaikitâyana Dâlbhya: 'O Dâlbhya, thy Sâman is not firmly established. And if any one were to say, Your head shall fall off (if you be wrong), surely your head would now fall.'

'And what is the origin of this world?'— He replied: 'Let no man carry the Sâman beyond this world as its rest. We place the Sâman in this world as its rest, for the Sâman is extolled as rest.'
8.8Then said Pravâhana Gaivali to Silaka Sâlâvatya: 'Your Sâman (the earth), O Sâlâvatya, has an end. And if any one were to say, Your head shall fall off (if you be wrong), surely your head would now fall.' 'Well then, let me know this from you, Sir,' said Sâlâvatya. 'Know it,' replied Gaivali.

9.2He is indeed the udgîtha (Om=Brahman), greater than great (parovarîyas), he is without end. He who knowing this meditates on the udgîtha, the greater than great, obtains what is greater than great, he conquers the worlds which are greater than great.
9.3Atidhanvan Saunaka, having taught this udgîtha to Udara-sândilya, said: 'As long as they will know in your family this udgîtha, their life in this world will be greater than great.

sa mā sarvair ārtvijyair vṛṇīteti ||
translation.text:
10.1When the Kurus had been destroyed by (hail) stones, Ushasti Kâkrâyana lived as a beggar with his virgin wife at Ibhyagrâma.
10.2Seeing a chief eating beans, he begged of him. The chief said: 'I have no more, except those which are put away for me here.'
10.3Ushasti said: 'Give me to eat of them.' He gave him the beans, and said: 'There is something to drink also.' Then said Ushasti: 'If I drank of it, I should have drunk what was left by another, and is therefore unclean.'
10.4The chief said: 'Were not those beans also left over and therefore unclean?' 'No,' he replied; 'for I should not have lived, if I had not eaten them, but the drinking of water would be mere pleasure.'
10.5Having eaten himself, Ushasti gave the remaining beans to his wife. But she, having eaten before, took them and put them away.
10.6Rising the next morning, Ushasti said to her: 'Alas, if we could only get some food, we might gain a little wealth. The king here is going to offer a sacrifice, he should choose me for all the priestly offices.'

10.7taṃ jāyovāca |
hanta pata ima eva kulmāṣā iti |
tān khāditvāmuṃ yajñaṃ vitatam eyāya ||
10.8tatrodgātḥn āstāve stoṣyamāṇān upopaviveśa |
sa ha prastotaram uvāca ||
10.9prastotar yā devatā prastāvam anvāyattā tāṃ ced avidvān prastoṣyasi mūrdhā te vipatiṣyatīti ||
10.10evam evodgātāram uvāca |
udgātar yā devatodgītham anvāyattā tāṃ ced avidvān udgāsyasi mūrdhā te vipatiṣyatīti ||
10.11evam eva pratihartāram uvāca |
pratihartar yā devatā pratihāram anvāyattā tāṃ ced avidvān pratihariṣyasi mūrdhā te vipatiṣyatīti |
te ha samāratās tūṣṇīm āsāṃ cakrire ||
translation.text:
10.7His wife said to him: 'Look, here are those beans of yours.' Having eaten them, he went to the sacrifice which was being performed.
10.8He went and sat down on the orchestra near the Udgâtris, who were going to sing their hymns of praise. And he said to the Prastotri (the leader):
10.9'Prastotri, if you, without knowing the deity which belongs to the prastâva (the hymns &c. of the Prastotri), are going to sing it, your head will fall off.'
10.10In the same manner he addressed the Udgâtri; 'Udgâtri, if you, without knowing the deity which belongs to the udgtîha (the hymns of the Udgâtri), are going to sing it, your head will fall off.'
10.11In the same manner he addressed the Pratihartri; 'Pratihartri, if you, without knowing the deity which belongs to the pratihâra (the hymns of the Pratihartri), are going to sing it, your head will fall off.' They stopped, and sat down in silence.

translation.original_text:
11.1atha hainaṃ yajamāna uvāca |
bhagavantaṃ vā ahaṃ vividiṣāṇīti |
uṣastir asmi cākrāyaṇa iti hovāca ||
11.2sa hovāca |
bhagavantaṃ vā aham ebhiḥ sarvair ārtvijyaiḥ paryaiṣiṣam |
bhagavato vā aham avittyānyān avṛṣi ||
11.3bhagavāṃs tv eva me sarvair ārtvijyair iti |
tatheti |
atha tarhy eta eva samatisṛṣṭāḥ stuvatām |
yāvat tv ebhyo dhanaṃ dadyās tāvan mama dadyā iti |
tatheti ha yajamāna uvāca ||
11.4atha hainaṃ prastotopasasāda |
prastotar yā devatā prastāvam anvāyattā tāṃ ced avidvān prastoṣyasi mūrdhā te vipatiṣyatīti mā bhagavān avocat |
katamā sā devateti ||
translation.text:
11.1Then the sacrificer said to him: 'I should like to know who you are, Sir.' He replied: 'I am Ushasti Kâkrâyana.'
11.2He said: 'I looked for you, Sir, for all these sacrificial offices, but not finding you, I chose others.'
11.3'But now, Sir, take all the sacrificial offices.' Ushasti said: "Very well; but let those, with my permission, perform the hymns of praise. Only as much wealth as you give to them, so much give to me also.' The sacrificer assented.
11.4Then the Prastotri approached him, saying: 'Sir, you said to me, "Prastotri, if you, without knowing the deity which belongs to the prastâva, are going to sing it, your head will fall off,"—which then is that deity?'

11.5prāṇa iti hovāca |
sarvāṇi ha vā imāni bhūtāni prāṇam evābhisaṃviśanti |
prāṇam abhyujjihate |
saiṣā devatā prastāvam anvāyattā |
tāṃ ced avidvān prāstoṣyo mūrdhā te vipatiṣyat tathoktasya mayeti ||
11.6atha hainam udgātopasasāda |
udgātar yā devatodgītham anvāyattā tāṃ ced avidvān udgāsyasi mūrdhā te vipatiṣyatīti mā bhagavān avocat |
katamā sā devatā iti ||
11.7āditya iti hovāca |
sarvāṇi ha vā imāni bhūtāny ādityam uccaiḥ santaṃ gāyanti |
saiṣā devatodgītham anvāyattā |
tāṃ ced avidvān udagāsyo mūrdhā te vyapatiṣyat tathoktasya mayeti ||
11.8atha hainaṃ pratihartopasasāda |
pratihartar yā devatā pratihāram anvāyattā tāṃ ced avidvān pratihariṣyasi mūrdhā te vipatiṣyatīti mā bhagavān avocat |
katamā sā devateti ||
translation.text:
11.5He said: 'Breath (prâna). For all these beings merge into breath alone, and from breath they arise. This is the deity belonging to the prastâva. If, without knowing that deity, you had sung forth your hymns, your head would have fallen off, after you had been warned by me.'
11.6Then the Udgâtri approached him, saying: 'Sir, you said to me, "Udgâtri, if you, without knowing the deity which belongs to the udgîtha, are going to sing it, your head will fall off,"—which then is that deity?'
11.7He said: 'The sun (âditya). For all these beings praise the sun when it stands on high. This is the deity belonging to the udgîtha. If without knowing that deity, you had sung out your hymns, your head would have fallen off, after you had been warned by me.'
11.8Then the Pratihartri approached him, saying: 'Sir, you said to me, "Pratihartri, if you, without knowing the deity belonging to the pratihâra, are going to sing it, your head will fall off,"—which then is that deity?'

12.2tasmai śvā śvetaḥ prādur babhūva |
tam anye śvāna upasametyocuḥ |
annaṃ no bhagavān āgāyatu |
aśanāyāma vā iti ||

tad dha bako dālbhyo glāvo vā maitreyaḥ pratipālayāṃ cakāra ||

te ha samupaviśya hiñ cakruḥ ||
12.5o3madā3ma |
oṃ3 pibā3ma |

annapate3'nnamihā2''harā2''haro3miti ||
translation.text:
11.9He said: 'Food (anna). For all these beings live when they partake of food. This is the deity belonging to the pratihâra. If, without knowing that deity, you had sung your hymns, your head would have fallen off, after you had been warned by me.'
12.1Now follows the udgîtha of the dogs. Vaka Dâlbhya, or, as he was also called, Glâva Maitreya, went out to repeat the Veda (in a quiet place).
12.2A white (dog) appeared before him, and other dogs gathering round him, said to him: 'Sir, sing and get us food, we are hungry.'
12.3The white dog said to them: 'Come to me to-morrow morning.' Vaka Dâlbhya, or, as he was also called, Glâva Maitreya, watched.
12.4The dogs came on, holding together, each dog keeping the tail of the preceding dog in his mouth, as the priests do when they are going to sing praises with the Vahishpavamâna hymn. After they had settled down, they began to say Hin.
12.5'Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink! Om, may the divine Varuna, Pragâpati, Savitri bring us food! Lord of food, bring hither food, bring it, Om!'

13.1ayaṃ vāva loko hāukāraḥ |
vāyur hāikāraḥ |
candramā athakāraḥ |
ātmehakāraḥ |
agnir īkāraḥ ||
13.2āditya ūkāraḥ |
nihava ekāraḥ |
viśve devā auhoyikāraḥ |
prajapatir hiṅkāraḥ |
prāṇaḥ svaraḥ |
annaṃ yā |
vāg virāṭ ||
13.3aniruktas trayodaśaḥ stobhaḥ saṃcaro huṅkāraḥ ||
13.4dugdhe 'smai vāg dohaṃ yo vāco dohaḥ |
annavān annādo bhavati |
ya etām evaṃ sāmnām upaniṣadaṃ vedopaniṣadaṃ veda ||
translation.text:
13.1The syllable Hâu is this world (the earth), the syllable Hâi the air, the syllable Atha the moon, the syllable Iha the self, the syllable Î is Agni, fire.
13.2The syllable Û is the sun, the syllable E is the Nihava or invocation, the syllable Auhoi is the Visve Devas, the syllable Hin is Pragâpati, Svara (tone) is breath (prâna), the syllable Yâ is food, the syllable Vâg is Virâg.
13.3The thirteenth stobha syllable, viz. the indistinct syllable Huṅ, is the Undefinable (the Highest Brahman).
13.4Speech yields the milk, which is the milk of speech itself to him who knows this Upanishad (secret doctrine) of the Sâmans in this wise. He becomes rich in food, and able to eat food,—yea, able to eat food.
